stories.text: If you live on Maui, you've probably passed this place hundreds of thousands of times. Kanaha Pond Wildlife Sanctuary, a peaceful haven for several species of water birds that are endemic or found only in Hawaiʻi. They coexist in this natural marshland. We have the indigenous ʻAkuʻu, the black-crowned night heron, a stately bird. The endangered Kāloa mauli, the Hawaiian duck. And here, I dare say, with my howly tongue, the ʻalee, keo keo, the Hawaiian coot, that doesn't seem to know whether it's coming or going. And above us, flying overhead in rather sloppy formation, the nene, the Hawaiian goose. And here she is, the greatly endangered star of the marsh, the queen of the marsh, the Hawaiian stilt. This entire sanctuary is called the home of the Hawaiian stilt. Look at her long, beautiful legs, perfectly suited for the environment. But it's not only birds that frequent the sanctuary. Beneath the surface of the water, there are pukas. And in each puka, there is a fish. Puka fish, I call them, because I don't know their real names. Something seems to be going on between the stilt and the duck. Perhaps they're in cahoots with the coot, looking for puka fish. And well, the Hawaiian The duck preens in the background. The Hawaiian stilt is looking for pokerfish. It won't take her long. It looks like she's come up with something. By Jove, it's a pokerfish. stories.text: This tiny tropical ice is not the victim of an enemy attack. It's the target, the United States Navy. One million pounds of TNT are detonated. To simulate the blast of an atomic bomb. The purpose of this Cold War experiment is to see how Navy ships could withstand a nuclear attack. Several large vessels are anchored close to shore. A monstrous explosion is powerful enough to wipe out a small city. Debris is sent flying more than half a mile into the day as the ships are engulfed in a thick cloud of dust. Watch as two surveillance blimps are blown out of the sky. Cameras mounted aboard the ships record the destruction. The shock waves are mighty enough to rip through steel walls. Heavy radar equipment is sent flying. A life-sized mannequin placed on the deck of one ship is blasted off its feet with frightening force. More than a minute later fragments of red-hot metal continue to rain down. Smoke clears revealing that somehow the ships have stayed afloat, but they are severely damaged. This simulation serves as an ominous example of the deadly and devastating power of nuclear weapons.

stories.headline: Flock owners unfamiliar with bird flu prevention; native birds endangered
stories.summary: A Department of Health survey found about two-thirds of flock owners did not know recommended bird flu prevention practices, followed by a segment on Hawaiʻi's endangered native birds.
stories.text: Seabirds such as albatrosses, terns, shearwaters, and petrels were the first to colonize the islands. These birds found a paradise devoid of predatory mammals and with no biting insects to spread disease. Many new species evolved, so it is shocking to learn that Hawaiʻi stands as one of the world's most graphic examples of an environmental disaster. Hawaiʻi can rightly be called the The third extinction capital of the world. No place on earth has experienced as many extinctions since human settlement. The reason is a prolonged cascade of harmful non-native animals and plants introduced to the islands by humans. The toll on native birds by non-native animals and plants over the past 200 years has been extraordinary. Cows, goats, sheep, and pigs spread into the native forests where they have methodically consumed native plants And degraded the native landscapes, often completely destroying native forests. Invasive non-native plants out-compete native species, often overwhelming whole forests and replacing them with single-species stands inhospitable to all but non-native birds. Just as Hawaiian birds evolved in the absence of predatory mammals, they also evolved in the absence of parasitic insects and the diseases they transmit. Mosquitoes are not native to Hawaiʻi. They were introduced back in the mid-1800s, along with two specific diseases, avian pox and avian malaria, which are both mosquito-borne. The native forest birds don't have any immunities to these diseases. For instance, Iiʻiwi, one bite from a malarial mosquito and they roll over dead in about three to four weeks. Only the Big Island and Maui now provide areas high enough to be truly mosquito- and disease-free. As a result, nearly all native forest birds have disappeared from Molokai, Lānaʻi, and Oahu. When I meet people who have lived on the islands their whole life, who saw the Nukupuʻu, who saw the Pouʻuʻuli and the Maui Akepa, and to think that I'll never see those and probably a lot of the young people on Maui will never see those birds again, I just would never want that to happen for the Maui Parrot Bill and the Akoi Koi and the Maui ʻAloha Hio. We really owe it to future generations to work harder than we've ever worked before to save these forests and the birds.

stories.text: You know, today is really about fulfilling a promise, a promise we made to our community here in Oʻolowalu, which was to move this from a temporary site and to move it to the permanent site. I tell you why that's an important promise, because nobody believed us. I mean, as government, if you don't keep your word, you don't have anything to rely on. We chose to have this temporary debris storage site To speed up the recovery effort throughout Lahaina. That way we can get back into rebuilding and recovering. And as we do this effort, we can then transfer the debris to its final location. So as a resident of Oluwalu, I was kind of on the fence, feeling about the temporary debris site being in Oluwalu. You know, a lot of my neighbors had concerns. However, because of my background and knowing how we were going to prepare the site, I was very confident that it was going to be a safe location to handle the debris. It was going to be managed correctly. There was going to be very minimal impact to the environment. We gave management and rights to the Army Corps of Engineers. So they actually prepared the site. They designed the site. They followed the Section 106 from the National Historic Preservation Division. All you have to do is turn around and look at the ocean. The near shore waters are so important for us to protect. ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, Kūpuna, ʻohana, kūpuna, mele, kūpuna, kūpuna, mele, k We're applying that same level of care where we want to minimize the impact and have the least amount of disruption to the community as we do it. One good example of a change that we made was to minimize the amount our vehicles are on public roads. And we've utilized the haul routes in order just to get them off these public roads as soon as possible just to both reduce the presence and reduce the impact. Just a little bit before lunch. There's actually quite a bit of surf today, so there's people in the water. There's a lot going on right here, but traffic's fine. So the Central Maui Landfill is very important in its location. It's far away from residential, it's far away from hospitals, schools. It's below or makai of the underground injection control line. What that line is, it's a demarcation between drinking water, underground drinking water, and non-drinking water. So it is above a non-drinking water source, so that's very critical. It's also critical for the environment because it's far away from near-shore waters, it's far away from the reefs, and it's also outside of the tsunami zone, which is very important when you have a facility like this. Once we're done with the hauling operations, we will return the temporary debris storage site to Maui County after it meets the restoration requirements. And once again, we get to that point where they're comfortable accepting this restored site, that's what we'll transfer it to them. Because we deal in the currency of trust with our community, that anytime and every time we keep our word, that builds the trust with our community as a whole. Even in big ways and small ways, and that it would speed up the recovery. So that was our goal was to speed it up, making good and delivering on the promise and the pledge we made to move it as soon as we could. And we know what it is that we're housing there. And we've also promised to keep that as a separate cell so it will not be mixed with any other household waste. So those are two things that we're very proud that we were able to accomplish. Very well done.

stories.text: What you need to know about sun safety. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States. Too much sun can cause skin cancer, which can be disfiguring and even deadly. Unprotected skin can be damaged by the sun's ultraviolet rays in as little as 15 minutes. Damage from exposure to UV rays builds up over a lifetime. Even on cloudy days, UV rays are present and can be reflected in water, sand, and snow. Stay in the shade. Especially during midday. Wear a hat with a wide brim to shade your face, head, ears, and neck. Wear sunglasses to block UVA and UVB rays. Wear clothing that covers your arms and legs. Every two hours apply sunscreen with SPF 15 or higher and UVA and UVB broad spectrum protection. Reapply sunscreen after swimming, sweating, or towel off. To learn more, visit cdc.gov, slash, cancer, slash, skin. Take care of yourselves and have a fun summer.

stories.text: We're on the big island of Hawaiʻi, right outside of a volcano. We are breeding endangered Hawaiian birds with the hope of someday releasing all of our species into the wild. Pretty much anything that could go wrong with Hawaiian birds went wrong with them, so a lot of loss of habitat, introduced predators, cats and rats. So the palila is found on this island, and the palila is kind of the, one of the hot bird issues of the Hawaiian islands right now. Their population is really seen to be crashing. In the early 2000s, their population was estimated at upwards of 4,000, and in this last survey, their population was under 2,000 birds. So their population really is going downhill. So, the palila is the last remaining seed eater of the Hawaiʻi honey creepers. So when the founding finches came to Hawaiʻi and then they all evolved into different seed eaters, insectivores, nectivores, the palila is the only seed eater that is not extinct. So almost all of their diet out in the wild is the endemic mamane tree, which is a legume seed pod you'd find up on the slopes of Mauna Kea. And unfortunately, the mamane tree was really affected by all The introduced ungulates, the introduced sheep and goats that are up on Mauna Kea, as well as the cattle, strip down the Maumāne tree and really destroy the tree and that's the only diet for palila. So, you know, that loss of their native plant and their native habitat has really affected those populations. And so until those areas are fenced off and the introduced ungulates are eradicated, the palila population is really going to be in jeopardy. Without people taking an interest in our work and being concerned about conservation in We won't be able to continue breeding as many ʻāla as we can, getting as many palila as we can for a large release cohort up here on Puʻu ʻMali. stories.headline: Maui Huliau segment on wish cycling: when in doubt, throw it out
stories.summary: After the host describes people putting non-recyclables in bins, a Maui Huliau segment explains what can and cannot be recycled on Maui.
stories.text: Well, news flash, because it's time to rewind on recycling, because today our recycling systems face a crisis. Wish cycling. But what's wish cycling? Why is it a crisis? And why should I care? Just like the name suggests, wish cycling is a combination of wishing and recycling. It's where things are put into the recycling with the hope that they're recyclable. And while done with good intentions to keep our ʻāina clean, these wish-cycle items become contamination and actually hurt our recycling systems as removing these items later is difficult and costly. So what is recyclable? Well, for plastics in Maui, only type 1 or 2 plastic with bottle-shaped necks and the caps taken off can be recycled. What's a type 1 or 2 plastic? You can find out what type of plastic something is made of by looking at the resin codes, those tiny numbers inside of recycling symbols on the bottom of most plastic. Unfortunately, most types of plastic are not actually recyclable, so it's always important to check which type you have before putting it in the recycling. Okay, so as long as this type one or two plastic, I can recycle it, right? Not quite. It needs to be bottle-shaped and have a neck. Wait, what? Does that mean my yogurt containers aren't recyclable? Nope. Or my egg carton? It's type 1 plastic. Not necessarily. It doesn't have a neck. Or my plastic salad container? My takeout box? Plastic bags, plastic straws, plastic cups, this diaper? Whoa! No, no, no, and definitely no. Well, what about my juice bottle? Or detergent bottle? Good call! However, before you can take those to the recycling, you need to make sure you rinse out any leftover food or substances and throw the lid away. However, you can recycle cardboard shipping boxes as long as you remove the plastic packaging inside, like this bubble wrap, which you can reuse when sending your next care package. Additionally, some companies will even accept returns of bubble package mailers, so they can reuse it in the future. Different shipping companies and locations will accept different things, so make sure to call ahead of time and double-check. However, if you can't reuse it, make sure you put it in the trash rather than recycling, so it doesn't become contamination. But it's not just plastic recycling you need to be conscious of. Make sure you double-check your cardboard. Anything with food residue in it needs to be thrown away, like this pizza box. Additionally, items made of mixed materials, like this oat milk carton made of a mix of cardboard and plastic, cannot be recycled and also needs to be sent to the landfill. We all want to keep our ʻāina clean, so be aware of what you can recycle. And, most importantly, always try to reduce your waste, especially plastic, by using reusable items as much as possible. Or alternative materials that can be composted or recycled. Recycling is not the answer to our waste problems. It's only a tiny part of the solution. Together, we can stop our recycling crisis. So remember, when it comes to recycling, if in doubt, throw it out.
